data.title: Thailand bans new Routledge textbook on contemporary politics, citing national security threats
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thailand bans new Routledge textbook on contemporary politics, citing national security threats
The Thai police have ordered a ban on the second edition of the Routledge Handbook of Contemporary Thailand, claiming that it contains chapters that could affect national security or cause unrest.
Edited by exiled academic Pavin Chachavalpongpun, the book contains chapters on the Thai military, the monarchy, and the use of the royal defamation law, as well as chapters on popular movements and other social and political issues. Pavin posted on Facebook on Thursday (5 November) that the book was banned for its content about the monarchy.
In a previous post, he wrote that book banning doesn’t work in the age of the internet, since people can buy e-books instead of hard copies. He also wrote that the ban would help promote the book.
Under the 2007 Printing Recordation Act, importing the book for distribution carries a prison sentence of up to three years, or a fine of up to 60,000 baht, or both. The police may also seize and destroy the book.
This is the second time one of Pavin’s publications has been banned in Thailand. In July 2023, the Thai authorities ordered a ban on his book “Rama X: The Thai Monarchy under King Vajiralongkorn” even before it was released.
iLaw noted that the police have banned six books since the Printing Recordation Act came into effect, all of which concerns the monarchy. Other than the two books by Pavin, the list includes:
Thailand’s Crisis and the Fight for Democracy by Giles Ungpakorn A Kingdom in Crisis by Andrew McGregor Marshall The November 2015 issue of the French edition of Marie Claire magazine The article “Thailand: Colossally Popular,” published in The New Age of the Kings: Modern Monarchies in Malaysia and the World

data.title: Detained activist goes on hunger strike to protest bail denial
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Detained activist goes on hunger strike to protest bail denial
Detained Activist Wanwalee Thammasattaya has gone on a hunger strike after she was denied bail and detained pending appeal on a royal defamation charge.
In a message released on her Facebook page, Wanwalee wrote that she has been on a hunger strike since 3 November. She insisted she is not a flight risk as she has attended every court appointment and that she has an uncle with terminal cancer and an elderly grandmother. She wrote that she will not eat until she is granted bail.
Wanwalee is among the five activists sentenced on 30 October to 2 years and 8 months in prison on a royal defamation charge filed against them over speeches given at a protest on 25 November 2020. Wanwalee was denied bail along with activist-turned-reporter Phongsatorn Tancharoen, while the remaining three activists were already detained at the time of the trial.
According to Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR), at least 33 people are detained on a royal defamation charge, 12 of whom are detained pending trial or appeal.

data.title: ECT challenges Supreme Court’s authority to examine Senate candidate qualifications
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
ECT challenges Supreme Court’s authority to examine Senate candidate qualifications
The Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) has sought a Constitutional Court ruling over the Supreme Court’s authority to examine the qualifications of Senate candidates, amid a controversy over the Senate selection fraud.
The ECT commissioners voted 5-2 to petition the Constitutional Court, asking it to rule whether the Supreme Court had the authority to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates, two of whom are sitting senators, according to several news outlets.
Three petitions were filed with the Supreme Court by unsuccessful Senate candidates, known as reserve senators. They asked the Court to examine the qualifications of five Senate candidates who had passed the preliminary qualification examination conducted by the ECT. The ECT had judged that these candidates were eligible after an earlier petition filed over their qualifications.
The Supreme Court began reviewing the evidence in October 2025. The Court is expected to conclude the case by the end of this year.
However, the majority of the ECT commissioners claim that by accepting the petitions, the Supreme Court has infringed on the ECT’s authority to oversee the Senate selection process, particularly as these candidates had been officially cleared by the commission.
According to the ECT, the Supreme Court has no authority to initiate on its own the process to revisit the ECT’s final decision.
On 4 November, the ECT filed its petition with the Constitutional Court. The ECT argues that the law narrowly defines the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction, and gives it no authority to initiate investigations into electoral fraud, except in cases referred to the Supreme Court by the ECT itself. This includes the case in which the ECT referred to the Court the case of 77 individuals allegedly involved in Senate selection fraud.

data.title: House Speaker rejects petition to proposal to repeal 1976 coup-era order
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
House Speaker rejects petition to proposal to repeal 1976 coup-era order
The House Speaker has rejected a petition initiating a bill to repeal an order made following the military coup of 1976 which increased the penalty for royal defamation.
iLaw reported that the October 6 Memorial Network submitted the petition to the House Speaker on 30 September. On 27 October, House Speaker Sophon Saram of the Bhumjaithai Party rejected the petition, arguing that citizens are not allowed to propose bills that are not related to people’s rights and freedom and this issue is instead a matter of state policy.
The Network said in a Facebook post that the bill, which is backed by over 59,000 people, aims to repeal an order made by the military junta that took power after the 1976 massacre at Thammasat University. It asks the legislature to reconsider an order that increased the penalties for a number of criminal offences, a matter which affects people’s rights and freedom.
The Network argued that penalties for criminal offences are directly related to constitutional rights and freedoms. The Constitution and a 2021 law on bills initiated by citizens requires that a bill be endorsed by at least 10,000 eligible voters before it can be introduced to Parliament. It must also be related in principle to constitutional provisions concerning the people‘s rights and freedoms or the duties of the state; this includes several provisions on the enforcement of criminal law as well as on freedom of expression.
It noted that the 2021 law shows that criminal law is not separate from constitutional freedoms, while the Constitution itself contains provisions controlling the state‘s exercise of its authority in criminal cases. In light of this, setting the penalty for a criminal offence is not solely a matter of state policy but also limits the people’s freedom. data.title: Activist found not guilty of royal defamation over graduation ceremony three-finger salute
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Activist found not guilty of royal defamation over graduation ceremony three-finger salute
The Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed a royal defamation charge filed against activist Songpol “Yajai” Sonthirak for flashing the three-finger salute at a graduation ceremony in December 2022.
Songpol was charged with royal defamation and violation of the Computer Crimes Act for flashing the three-finger “Hunger Games” salute, a well-known resistance symbol used by activists protesting the 2014 military coup and by students in the 2020 pro-democracy movement, after receiving his degree certificate from Princess Sirindhorn, King Vajiralongkorn’s younger sister, during Khon Kaen University’s graduation ceremony on 20 December 2022. He was also charged for an interview with The Isaan Record and another with a Khon Kaen University student activist group. He was indicted in November 2025.
Khon Kaen University reportedly paused its live broadcast of the graduation ceremony while Songpol and subsequent graduates from the Faculty of Law were receiving their certificates, and did not allow comments on the live broadcast after it resumed.
The complaint against him was filed by Kamon Kitkasiwat, leader of a royalist group in Khon Kaen, who was at the time an MP candidate for the royalist Thai Pakdee Party.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said today (10 November) that the Khon Kaen Provincial Court has dismissed the charge against Songpol. It ruled that, given his behaviour before the ceremony and that he is part of the same activist group as Jatupat Boonpattararaksa, flashing the three-finger salute in front of Princess Sirindhorn can be seen as anti-monarchy, but while it is disrespectful and an insult, it is not defamatory. The princess is also not covered by the royal defamation law, which only covers the King, the Queen, the heir to the throne, and the regent. data.title: Appeal Court ruling puts Election Commission under renewed legal pressure
data.author: eng editor 3
data.summary:
Appeal Court ruling puts Election Commission under renewed legal pressure
The Appeal Court has ruled that members of the public can directly file criminal lawsuits against Election Commission of Thailand (ECT) officials over alleged malfeasance in the 2024 Senate selection, bypassing the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), which normally investigate allegations before cases can proceed to court.
The case stems from a lawsuit filed by a Senate candidate Phongsakorn Tangkittrakul against seven Election commissioners and ECT Secretary-General Sawaeng Boonme at the Chon Buri Provincial Court, accusing the eight of malfeasance for allowing the 2024 Senate selection to proceed without transparency and fairness.
The case was later referred to the Appeal Court President to determine whether it was within the Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct’s jurisdiction.
The Appeal Court ruling, issued on 6 November, stated that the Senate selection process misappropriated the sovereign power of Thai citizens, who were collectively victimised in the process, leaving them at liberty to bypass the NACC and directly file lawsuits against officials involved with the Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct.
The ruling overturned an earlier 5 May decision by the previous President which rejected Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct jurisdiction over the case.
According to Section 235 of the Constitution, a case which involves allegations against individuals holding positions in the independent institutions, including Constitutional Court and the ECT, must first be submitted to the NACC for further investigation. The NACC will then determine whether there are sufficient grounds to refer it on to the Criminal Court for Corruption and Misconduct.
The Organic Act on Criminal Procedure of Persons Holding Political Positions further stipulates that proceedings should be initiated by the Attorney-General or the NACC commissioners.

data.title: Thaksin amnesty petition awaits review
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Thaksin amnesty petition awaits review
Former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra has applied for amnesty under the new Amnesty Act. His lawyer said he is seeking to clear his name to spend his old age out of politics.
Thaksin’s lawyer, Winyat Chatmontree, said Thaksin authorised him to file a petition on his behalf on 8 October through the joint service center of the Office of the Permanent Secretary, Prime Minister’s Office. The petition requested the Committee on Promoting a Peaceful Society to rule whether he is eligible for amnesty under the new amnesty law for political participation, formally called the Promotion of a Peaceful Society Act. Winyat said Thaksin is seeking to clear his name and that he does not wish to be involved in politics as he is getting older.
Thaksin is seeking amnesty for several corruption and misconduct charges filed against him for the 4-billion-Baht EXIM Bank loan, the two- and three-digit lottery project, the Shin Satellite concession modifications, and the 46-billion-Baht asset seizure. Amnesty would expunge his criminal records, and relieve him from all legal liabilities resulting from previous convictions. On 14 October, Winyat told The Nation that the petition covers cases he described as politically motivated and does not include the royal defamation charge for which Thaksin was acquitted in August 2025 and prosecutors have since appealed. He acknowledged that critics argue Thaksin’s convictions may fall within the law’s exclusions, particularly those covering corruption and misconduct, but stressed that filing a petition does not automatically entitle him to amnesty.
Piyasiri Wattanavrangkul, the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Justice, said on 26 October that the Committee on Promoting a Peaceful Society will consider Thaksin’s petition during its meeting in November. As chair of the screening subcommittee, Piyasiri said that he would convene a meeting as soon as possible once the subcommittee received his petition.

data.title: Man indicted for royal defamation over FB posts, denied bail
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
Man indicted for royal defamation over FB posts, denied bail
Nattakan Jaiaree, a 40-year-old motorcycle taxi driver, has been denied bail after he was indicted on a royal defamation charge over three Facebook posts made in 2022.
Thai Lawyers for Human Rights (TLHR) said Nattakan was indicted on 10 November. The Phatthalung Provincial Court denied him bail on the grounds that the offence is serious and he is likely to repeat it.
TLHR noted that the court believes he is likely to be a repeat offender although he has not been found guilty and has no other royal defamation charge against him.
The complaint against Nattakan was filed by Songchai Niamhom, leader of the ultra-royalist King Protection Group. Songchai is a known serial royal defamation complainant who has filed at least 19 royal defamation and sedition complaints against activists and social media users with the police in several southern provinces. Many of the accused do not live in the south and so are forced to shoulder the burden of travel costs to attend court appointments.
On 6 November 2023, Nattakan was arrested in Bangkok. TLHR said that police summonses were sent to a house he no longer lived in and he was not aware he had been summoned. He was taken to Phatthalung the next day. The police then informed him of the charges. The Phatthalung Provincial Court subsequently denied him bail on the grounds that the charges carry a high penalty and because he does not have a permanent residence and is likely to repeat his offence. He was detained for 84 days and was released on 1 February 2024 after the public prosecutor did not indict him within the time limit allowed for detention pending investigation.
In mid-2026, Nattakan was unable to get a new identification card. He then learned of an outstanding arrest warrant issued by the Phatthalung Provincial Court on 1 August 2025. data.title: World leaders should increase pressure on Myanmar junta to end abuses, says Human Rights Watch
data.author: eng editor 1
data.summary:
World leaders should increase pressure on Myanmar junta to end abuses, says Human Rights Watch
World leaders gathering in the Philippines on November 15-17, 2026, should more forcefully address the human rights and humanitarian crisis in Myanmar, Human Rights Watch said on 11 November. The East Asia Summit and Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and partner summits will include leaders of ASEAN nations and the United States, European Union, Japan, China, and India, among other countries.
In a November 5 letter to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines, the ASEAN chair and summit host, Human Rights Watch urged ASEAN not to recognize or endorse the sham elections earlier in 2026 that resulted in junta leader Min Aung Hlaing assuming Myanmar’s presidency. In recent months, several governments in ASEAN and the region have hosted Min Aung Hlaing, despite the junta’s rejection of ASEAN’s calls to address human rights and humanitarian issues. On November 11, the Philippine government confirmed that Min Aung Hlaing would not attend the summit. ASEAN partners should urge the bloc to continue blocking junta officials from representing Myanmar at ASEAN meetings, Human Rights Watch said.
“ASEAN could play an important role in bringing a stop to Myanmar military abuses,” said John Sifton, Asia advocacy director at Human Rights Watch. “Governments should be increasing pressure on the junta to end its attacks on civilians, lift restrictions on humanitarian aid, and begin credible dialogues about transitioning to civilian rule.”
As commander-in-chief of Myanmar’s military both before and after its 2021 military coup, Min Aung Hlaing has led numerous abusive military operations throughout the country, many including war crimes and crimes against humanity.
